intents: a wave of angry public reaction against a decision or change
when a company changes something and crowds of customers push back hard and loudly
the angry pushback that makes people regret what they announced
ru_cue: резкое недовольство публики после нового решения или поступка

upgrades.plain: When the school changed the uniform, there was [a big angry reaction] from parents.
upgrades.better: When the school changed the uniform, there was a *backlash* from parents.

upgrades.plain: His joke at the wedding caused [a wave of anger] online, and his sister still hasn't forgiven him.
upgrades.better: His joke at the wedding caused a *backlash* online, and his sister still hasn't forgiven him.

upgrades.plain: The café raised its prices and quickly backed down after [regulars got angry and complained].
upgrades.better: The café raised its prices and quickly backed down after a *backlash* from regulars.

ru_trap: Russian 'реакция на' tempts 'a backlash on'; English says a backlash against or over something.
nuance: Always negative and collective: many people turning against something, not one person's reply.
personal: Can you remember a decision at your school or work that caused a backlash?
Has anyone you know ever faced a backlash for something they said or posted?
hook: Back + lash: crack a whip and it lashes back into your own face.

intents: decide what to do as things happen, instead of planning ahead
when you've booked nothing for the weekend and will just see what the weather does
stay flexible and react to the situation rather than fix a plan
ru_cue: ничего не планировать заранее и решать по ходу дела

upgrades.plain: We haven't booked anything for Saturday, so let's just [see how it goes].
upgrades.better: We haven't booked anything for Saturday, so let's just *play it by ear*.

upgrades.plain: I don't know how long the meeting will last, so I'll [decide on the day] about dinner.
upgrades.better: I don't know how long the meeting will last, so I'll *play it by ear* about dinner.

upgrades.plain: My mum wanted a full schedule for her visit, but with a newborn we had to [take each hour as it came].
upgrades.better: My mum wanted a full schedule for her visit, but with a newborn we had to *play it by ear*.

collocations.chunk: let's just play it by ear
we'll have to play it by ear

nuance: Keep the 'it': 'play by ear' alone means playing music without notes. Casual, not for formal writing.
personal: When did you last play it by ear on a trip, and how did it turn out?
Who do you know who always plays it by ear and never makes plans?
gesture: Cup a hand behind your ear, then shrug and wave the other hand forward: we'll see.
hook: A musician with no sheet music just listens and plays along; you have no plan and follow what happens.

intents: giving up some of one good thing to get more of another
when the cheaper flight saves money but leaves at four in the morning, so you have to choose
the price you pay in one area for a gain in another, like speed against quality
ru_cue: выигрываешь в одном, но обязательно теряешь в другом

upgrades.plain: The cheaper flight leaves at four in the morning; that's [the price you pay] for saving money.
upgrades.better: The cheaper flight leaves at four in the morning; that's the *trade-off* for saving money.

upgrades.plain: Moving closer to work means a smaller flat, and we argued for weeks about whether [giving up the space for the time] was worth it.
upgrades.better: Moving closer to work means a smaller flat, and we argued for weeks about whether the *trade-off* was worth it.

upgrades.plain: There's always [a balance you have to strike] between speed and quality.
upgrades.better: There's always a *trade-off* between speed and quality.

collocations.chunk: a trade-off between cost and quality

ru_trap: Russian 'компромисс' covers both; in English a compromise is people meeting halfway, a trade-off is giving up one quality for another.
nuance: A trade-off is a choice between two good things; a drawback is just the downside of one thing.
personal: What trade-off did you make when you chose where to live or study?
What trade-off has someone in your family made for their job?
gesture: Hold both hands out like scales; lift one as the other sinks.
hook: A market trader: 'I'll trade you this off for that': you only get one thing by handing over another.

intents: the freedom to make your own decisions without anyone controlling you
when your boss lets your team run its own budget and nobody checks every step
being in charge of your own work or life instead of answering to someone above you
ru_cue: свобода самому решать, как действовать, без чужого контроля

upgrades.plain: What I love about working from home is [being free to decide things myself].
upgrades.better: What I love about working from home is the *autonomy*.

upgrades.plain: Teachers want more [freedom to decide] how they run their classes.
upgrades.better: Teachers want more *autonomy* over how they run their classes.

upgrades.plain: When he lost his licence, my grandad felt he'd lost [his independence], and he hated asking us for lifts.
upgrades.better: When he lost his licence, my grandad felt he'd lost his *autonomy*, and he hated asking us for lifts.

ru_trap: Russian 'автономность' of a phone or laptop is 'battery life' in English, not autonomy.
nuance: Autonomy is the right to decide for yourself; independence can also just mean not needing help or money.
personal: How much autonomy do you have in your study or work right now?
Who do you know who would hate to lose their autonomy?
hook: Auto, as in automobile: it moves by itself, and with autonomy you steer yourself.

intents: the roads, pipes, power lines and internet a town needs to work
when a new housing estate goes up but there are no buses, no school and a weak water supply
the basic physical systems under everyday life that you only notice when they fail
ru_cue: дороги, транспорт, связь, водопровод и все, без чего город не может работать

upgrades.plain: The town needs better [roads, pipes and transport] before more houses are built.
upgrades.better: The town needs better *infrastructure* before more houses are built.

upgrades.plain: The government is spending billions on [roads, railways and bridges].
upgrades.better: The government is spending billions on *infrastructure*.

upgrades.plain: We moved to the village for some peace, but [the internet and the buses] are so bad that I nearly missed my own job interview.
upgrades.better: We moved to the village for some peace, but the *infrastructure* is so bad that I nearly missed my own job interview.

nuance: Usually uncountable and physical: the roads, networks and utilities themselves, not the services run on them.
personal: What is the worst thing about the infrastructure where you live?
Who do you know who complains most about local infrastructure, and what about?
hook: Infra means 'below': the structure below the city, all the pipes and cables under the street.

intents: how common something is across a whole group or area
when doctors count how many office workers out of every hundred have back pain
the share of people or places affected by something, often a problem
ru_cue: то, насколько часто что-то встречается среди людей или в каком-то месте

upgrades.plain: Doctors are worried about [how common back pain is] among office workers.
upgrades.better: Doctors are worried about the *prevalence* of back pain among office workers.

upgrades.plain: The surveyor was surprised by [how many old flats had damp].
upgrades.better: The surveyor was surprised by the *prevalence* of damp in old flats.

upgrades.plain: My essay was due in an hour and I still couldn't find any figures on [how common the illness is] in each region.
upgrades.better: My essay was due in an hour and I still couldn't find any figures on the *prevalence* of the illness in each region.

nuance: The noun behind prevalent: it measures how common something is (high, low, rising), so it suits figures and studies.
personal: Which habit do you think has the highest prevalence among people your age?
Has anyone you know, like a doctor or a teacher, talked about the prevalence of a problem at their work?
hook: Like Russian 'превалировать': the thing that prevails and turns up everywhere you look.

intents: getting the advantages of two different options at once, without their usual downsides
when you live near fields and woods but are still only twenty minutes from the city centre
a happy situation where you don't have to choose between two good things
ru_cue: получить плюсы двух разных вариантов сразу и не мириться с их минусами

upgrades.plain: Living just outside the city gives you [the good parts of town and country].
upgrades.better: Living just outside the city gives you *the best of both worlds*.

upgrades.plain: Working two days at home and three in the office is [perfect, because I get the advantages of each].
upgrades.better: Working two days at home and three in the office is *the best of both worlds*.

upgrades.plain: My parents argued for years about the city or a village, and a cottage near the station finally gave them [what each of them wanted].
upgrades.better: My parents argued for years about the city or a village, and a cottage near the station finally gave them *the best of both worlds*.

collocations.chunk: it gives you the best of both worlds
you can't have the best of both worlds

ru_trap: Russian has no article here; English always keeps it: the best of both worlds.
nuance: Only for a happy mix of two options; if you must give one up to get the other, it's a trade-off instead.
personal: Is there anything in your life that gives you the best of both worlds?
Who do you know who seems to have the best of both worlds?
hook: Picture two planets, and you pick the ripest fruit from each without leaving your chair.

intents: a long stretch of serious hardship and bad luck that you have to get through
the hardship a family faces when it loses its home and then its income
the tough conditions life throws at you: the hardship itself, not how well you cope
ru_cue: долгие тяжелые испытания, через которые приходится проходить

upgrades.plain: She stayed cheerful through years of [hard times].
upgrades.better: She stayed cheerful through years of *adversity*.

upgrades.plain: The team showed real courage [when everything was going against them].
upgrades.better: The team showed real courage in the face of *adversity*.

upgrades.plain: My dad never talks about the [tough times] he went through as a child, but I think it's why he never gives up.
upgrades.better: My dad never talks about the *adversity* he went through as a child, but I think it's why he never gives up.

ru_trap: Russian 'невзгоды' is plural, but English adversity is usually uncountable: 'years of adversity', not 'adversities'.
nuance: Adversity is the hardship you face; resilience is your ability to bounce back from it.
personal: What adversity have you faced that made you stronger?
Who in your family dealt with adversity in a way you admire?
hook: 'Ад-versity': a university in hell (ад) where every course is hardship.

intents: the ability to bounce back quickly after a setback or a shock
when you fail an exam, feel awful for a day, then pick yourself up and try again
the inner toughness that lets a person or a community recover instead of breaking
ru_cue: умение быстро прийти в себя и снова встать на ноги после удара

upgrades.plain: Children build [the ability to bounce back] by failing sometimes and trying again.
upgrades.better: Children build *resilience* by failing sometimes and trying again.

upgrades.plain: After losing her job and her flat in the same month, her [ability to pick herself up] amazed all of us.
upgrades.better: After losing her job and her flat in the same month, her *resilience* amazed all of us.

upgrades.plain: The team showed real [toughness] after going two goals down.
upgrades.better: The team showed real *resilience* after going two goals down.

nuance: Resilience is recovering after a blow; robust describes something strong enough not to be damaged in the first place.
personal: When did you need the most resilience in your life so far?
Who is the person with the most resilience that you know?
gesture: Press your palm down on an imaginary spring, then let your hand bounce back up.
hook: 'Резил-' sounds like резина (rubber): rubber gets squashed and springs back into shape.

intents: a situation that sounds as if it contradicts itself but turns out to be true
a situation like this one: the busiest person you know is always the one who has time to help
a strange contradiction in a fact or statement that makes you stop and puzzle over it
ru_cue: явное противоречие, которое при этом оказывается правдой

upgrades.plain: It's [a puzzling contradiction] that the busiest people often find time to help.
upgrades.better: It's a *paradox* that the busiest people often find time to help.

upgrades.plain: [The odd contradiction] is that spending less took more effort.
upgrades.better: The *paradox* is that spending less took more effort.

upgrades.plain: Here's [the strange contradiction]: the more I tried to relax before my exam, the more nervous I got.
upgrades.better: Here's the *paradox*: the more I tried to relax before my exam, the more nervous I got.

nuance: Paradox is the noun for the contradiction itself; paradoxically introduces one inside a sentence.
personal: What paradox have you noticed in your own habits?
Which person you know is a walking paradox, and why?
hook: 'Пара доков': a pair of doctors say opposite things, and somehow both are right.

intents: splitting something into two opposite camps as if there were nothing in between
when someone insists you're either a city person or a country person and can't be a bit of each
a sharp either-or contrast between two ideas, like work against rest or art against craft
ru_cue: деление на две противоположности, как будто третьего не дано

upgrades.plain: There's [a false either-or] between working hard and resting well.
upgrades.better: There's a false *dichotomy* between working hard and resting well.

upgrades.plain: The film explores [the split] between duty and desire.
upgrades.better: The film explores the *dichotomy* between duty and desire.

upgrades.plain: My dad keeps insisting I'm either 'creative' or 'good at maths', and I'm tired of [that black-and-white split].
upgrades.better: My dad keeps insisting I'm either 'creative' or 'good at maths', and I'm tired of that *dichotomy*.

collocations.chunk: the dichotomy between duty and desire

nuance: A dichotomy is a two-way split into opposites; a disparity is an unfair gap between groups.
personal: Which dichotomy do people wrongly apply to you, like 'sporty or clever'?
Who do you know who sees everything as a dichotomy, with no middle ground?
gesture: Chop one hand straight down in front of you, then push the two halves apart.
hook: Di = two, -tomy = cut, as in a surgeon's operation: one knife stroke, two opposite halves.

intents: share the same opinion as someone, often said of two people who usually clash
when you and your sister, who argue about everything, finally hold the same opinion on something
have matching views on something people often argue about, like money or politics
ru_cue: иметь одинаковое мнение с кем-то, особенно в спорном вопросе

upgrades.plain: We don't [agree] about politics, but we get on well.
upgrades.better: We don't *see eye to eye* about politics, but we get on well.

upgrades.plain: My mum and my wife have never [agreed about anything], so Christmas dinner is always tense.
upgrades.better: My mum and my wife have never *seen eye to eye*, so Christmas dinner is always tense.

upgrades.plain: My brother and I [have completely different opinions] on how to raise kids, so we just avoid the subject.
upgrades.better: My brother and I don't *see eye to eye* on how to raise kids, so we just avoid the subject.

collocations.chunk: don't see eye to eye on money
never really saw eye to eye
see eye to eye with his father

ru_trap: Russian 'сходиться в чем-то' tempts 'see eye to eye in'; English says on or about: see eye to eye on money.
nuance: About opinions, and mostly used in the negative ('we don't see eye to eye'); on the same page is about sharing an understanding of a plan.
personal: On what topic do you rarely see eye to eye with people your age?
Which family member do you never see eye to eye with, and about what?
gesture: Point two fingers at your own eyes, then level them at someone else's eyes at the same height.
hook: Two people exactly the same height, eyes level, looking at the world from the same spot.

intents: a small, subtle difference in meaning, tone or feeling that's easy to miss
when a joke stops being funny after translation because something delicate gets lost
the fine shades in what someone says that a quick summary leaves out
ru_cue: тонкое, едва заметное отличие в смысле или интонации

upgrades.plain: Jokes often lose their [subtle meaning] when you translate them.
upgrades.better: Jokes often lose their *nuance* when you translate them.

upgrades.plain: The argument has more [fine detail] than the headline suggests.
upgrades.better: The argument has more *nuance* than the headline suggests.

upgrades.plain: I missed [the small shift] in her tone when she said 'fine', and we ended up having a huge row.
upgrades.better: I missed the *nuance* in her tone when she said 'fine', and we ended up having a huge row.

ru_trap: Russian 'есть один нюанс' means 'there's a catch'; English nuance is a subtle shade of meaning, never a problem.
nuance: A compliment to precision: a nuance is a delicate shade, not a hidden problem or a big difference.
personal: Which nuance of English do you still find hardest to hear?
Who do you know who always picks up the nuance in what people say?
hook: 'New ounce': one new ounce of salt changes the soup only slightly, but a good cook notices.

intents: a moment when something important suddenly becomes clear and changes how you see things
when you're washing up and it hits you that you don't want that job at all
a lightbulb moment that comes from inside you, not from a shock or a warning
ru_cue: миг, когда тебя вдруг осеняет и все видится по-новому

upgrades.plain: Standing on the beach, I [suddenly realised] I didn't want that job at all.
upgrades.better: Standing on the beach, I had an *epiphany*: I didn't want that job at all.

upgrades.plain: [The sudden realisation] came while he was washing up.
upgrades.better: The *epiphany* came while he was washing up.

upgrades.plain: At four in the morning, the night before my deadline, I had [a sudden flash of understanding] about how to fix the whole essay.
upgrades.better: At four in the morning, the night before my deadline, I had an *epiphany* about how to fix the whole essay.

collocations.chunk: had an epiphany about my career

nuance: An epiphany comes from inside, in a flash; a wake-up call is a shock from outside that warns you.
personal: When did you last have an epiphany, and what was it about?
Has anyone you know had an epiphany that changed their life?
gesture: Freeze, then flick your fingers open beside your head like a lightbulb switching on.
hook: 'Эпи-фонарь': a lantern (фонарь) suddenly lights up in your head.

intents: a natural feeling of connection with something or someone, as if it just suits you
when you walk into a town for the first time and feel strangely at home
being naturally drawn to something, like languages, animals or numbers
ru_cue: естественная тяга к чему-то, ощущение, что тебе это по-настоящему близко

upgrades.plain: I've always had [a natural connection] with cats; they seem to trust me.
upgrades.better: I've always had an *affinity* with cats; they seem to trust me.

upgrades.plain: He has [a natural feel] for languages.
upgrades.better: He has a natural *affinity* for languages.

upgrades.plain: My parents wanted me to study law, but I'd always felt [drawn to] art, and telling them was the hardest conversation of my life.
upgrades.better: My parents wanted me to study law, but I'd always felt an *affinity* with art, and telling them was the hardest conversation of my life.

ru_trap: Russian 'к' tempts 'affinity to'; English says an affinity with or for something.
nuance: A calm, natural fit rather than strong love or desire; you can feel an affinity with a place, a style or a group of people.
personal: What subject or place have you always felt an affinity with?
Who do you know who has a real affinity for animals or children?
hook: 'A fin-ity': a fish's fin just belongs in water, a natural fit.

intents: so clear and bright in your mind that you can almost see it again
when a friend describes a market so well that you can picture every stall
full of strong colour and sharp detail, like a dream you remember perfectly
ru_cue: такой яркий и четкий, что легко представить перед глазами

upgrades.plain: She gave such a [detailed, clear] description that I could picture the room.
upgrades.better: She gave such a *vivid* description that I could picture the room.

upgrades.plain: The dream was so [real and clear] that she wrote it down.
upgrades.better: The dream was so *vivid* that she wrote it down.

upgrades.plain: I still have a [very clear] memory of the moment I forgot my lines in the school play.
upgrades.better: I still have a *vivid* memory of the moment I forgot my lines in the school play.

ru_trap: Russian 'яркий' also covers a bright lamp or a lively person; for light say bright, keep vivid for colours, memories and descriptions.
nuance: Vivid is about how clearly something appears to the eye or the mind; luminous is about light actually glowing.
personal: What is your most vivid childhood memory?
Who do you know with the most vivid imagination?
hook: Vivid sounds like 'видел' (saw): you remember it as if you had just seen it.

intents: an idea that's worth turning over in your head for a while after you hear it
when a friend's passing comment about your screen time keeps you reflecting all the way home
something that doesn't give you an answer but makes you reconsider
ru_cue: то, над чем стоит хорошенько поразмыслить

upgrades.plain: Her comment about spending less time online really [made me think].
upgrades.better: Her comment about spending less time online really gave me *food for thought*.

upgrades.plain: The talk gave everyone [a lot to think about].
upgrades.better: The talk gave everyone plenty of *food for thought*.

upgrades.plain: My teacher's remark that I only work when someone's watching stung, but it was [something worth thinking about].
upgrades.better: My teacher's remark that I only work when someone's watching stung, but it was *food for thought*.

collocations.chunk: it gave me food for thought

ru_trap: No article: 'that's food for thought', not 'a food for thought'.
nuance: Slow and open: it gives you material to reflect on, unlike an epiphany, which is a sudden answer.
personal: What gave you real food for thought recently?
Who do you know whose advice usually gives you food for thought?
hook: Picture a sandwich for your brain: something to chew on slowly.

intents: making you feel you're right inside it, so the real world around you fades away
when a video game pulls you in so deeply that you forget to eat
surrounding you on every side with sound, images or a language, so you're in it rather than watching
ru_cue: дающий ощущение, что ты сам внутри происходящего

upgrades.plain: The game [pulls you in] so much that I forget to eat.
upgrades.better: The game is so *immersive* that I forget to eat.

upgrades.plain: The course offers [a week where you hear nothing but Spanish].
upgrades.better: The course offers an *immersive* week in Spanish.

upgrades.plain: I dragged my dad to the exhibition expecting him to be bored, but it felt so [much like being inside the scene] that he didn't want to leave.
upgrades.better: I dragged my dad to the exhibition expecting him to be bored, but it was so *immersive* that he didn't want to leave.

collocations.frame: the game creates a truly ___ world

nuance: About being surrounded and drawn inside (games, theatre, language courses); vivid only describes clear images.
personal: What is the most immersive book, game or film you have ever experienced?
Who do you know who learned a language through an immersive stay abroad?
hook: 'Им-МОРЕ-сив': you're under the sea (море), and water surrounds you on every side.

intents: making you feel thrilled, breathless and full of energy
when you race down a hill on a bike with the wind in your face and can't stop grinning
so exciting that you feel more alive than usual, often with a bit of speed or danger
ru_cue: вызывающий бурный восторг и ощущение, что ты по-настоящему жив

upgrades.plain: Swimming in the sea in winter is freezing but [really exciting].
upgrades.better: Swimming in the sea in winter is freezing but *exhilarating*.

upgrades.plain: The ride down the hill was [so exciting I couldn't stop laughing].
upgrades.better: The ride down the hill was *exhilarating*.

upgrades.plain: After months of rehearsals and nearly quitting twice, singing on that stage was [an amazing feeling].
upgrades.better: After months of rehearsals and nearly quitting twice, singing on that stage was *exhilarating*.

nuance: Stronger and more physical than exciting (speed, cold water, height). The experience is exhilarating; you feel exhilarated.
personal: What is the most exhilarating thing you have ever done?
Who do you know who finds dangerous sports exhilarating?
hook: Ex-HILL-arating: flying down a hill, the wind blows the breath right out of you.

intents: so big or hard that it shakes your confidence before you even start
when you look at the huge pile of forms on day one and wonder whether you can even begin
making you feel small and unsure, like looking up at a mountain you're about to climb
ru_cue: такой сложный на вид, что заранее пропадает уверенность в себе

upgrades.plain: Starting a new job is [scary], especially in the first week.
upgrades.better: Starting a new job is *daunting*, especially in the first week.

upgrades.plain: The thought of giving a speech at my sister's wedding was [really scary], and I nearly said no.
upgrades.better: The thought of giving a speech at my sister's wedding was *daunting*, and I nearly said no.

upgrades.plain: The task seemed [so scary that we didn't even want to start] until we split it up.
upgrades.better: The task seemed *daunting* until we split it up.

nuance: Daunting is how a task looks before you start; arduous is how hard it is to keep going once you have.
personal: What task feels most daunting to you right now?
Who do you know who took on something daunting and managed it?
gesture: Lean back and slowly look up, as if at a huge wall right in front of you.
hook: 'Донт' (don't): the mountain looks down at you and says 'don't even try'.

intents: so worried and out of options that you'll try anything
when you've been lost in the rain for hours and would get on any bus at all
needing something urgently and badly, like sleep, work or help, right now
ru_cue: когда все варианты кончились и ты готов на что угодно

upgrades.plain: After three hours lost in the rain, we [really, really wanted] to find a bus stop.
upgrades.better: After three hours lost in the rain, we were *desperate* to find a bus stop.

upgrades.plain: He [badly needed] work after six months without a job.
upgrades.better: He was *desperate* for work after six months without a job.

upgrades.plain: She sounded [panicked and helpless] on the phone, so I drove straight over.
upgrades.better: She sounded *desperate* on the phone, so I drove straight over.

collocations.chunk: desperate for a decent night's sleep

ru_trap: Russian 'отчаянный' can mean daring ('отчаянный парень'); English desperate never means brave, only hopeless or in urgent need.
nuance: Urgent and anxious: you need it now and will try anything; yearn is a slow, deep longing.
personal: When were you last desperate for something, and what did you do?
Who do you know who once made a desperate attempt to fix a mistake?
hook: 'Despair-ate': despair ate up all your options, so you grab at anything.
